author: Carlos Martinez
title: When to Buy Sim Racing Gear: Seasonal Sales Strategy Guide
description: Map out the best times to buy wheels, pedals and cockpits. Learn which sales periods offer real discounts and which are marketing noise.

sections.p: Sim racing hardware costs real money. A direct drive wheelbase alone runs ~$400 to ~$1200, and once you commit to pedals, a wheel, and a cockpit frame, you are looking at a serious capital outlay. Timing that purchase around actual sales events instead of impulse buying or random discounts can save hundreds of dollars and let you upgrade more frequently or invest in better gear than you planned. The trick is knowing which sales are genuinely profitable and which are inflated retail windows disguised as deals.

Unlike consumer electronics that follow a strict refresh calendar, sim racing hardware sales depend on a mix of retail seasons, gaming events, and manufacturer stock cycles. A MOZA R9 might see a modest discount in October but a steeper one in March. The same applies to most components. This guide maps the actual sales windows across a calendar year and explains why each one exists, so you can plan your purchase rather than chase phantom discounts.

sections.h2: Black Friday and Cyber Monday (late November)

sections.p: Black Friday and Cyber Monday remain the most heavily marketed sim racing sales events. Major retailers and manufacturers do participate, but discounts are often modest: 10 to 20 percent is common, and anything over 25 percent is rare. The real value lies in the breadth of discounts across multiple brands at once, making it easy to compare multiple wheelbases, pedals, or cockpit frames in one shopping window.

The catch is that Black Friday discounts rely on retail markup, so you must know baseline prices before the event. A wheel listed at an inflated MSRP during October, then discounted 20 percent for Black Friday, may still be more expensive than its actual street price in January. Watch prices in September and early October to establish what a fair retail price looks like. Also be aware that popular items sell out fast: limited inventory is the norm, not the exception.

list: Check baseline prices at major retailers (Amazon, NewEgg, Best Buy, B&H Photo) in September and October.
Set up price alerts on sites like CamelCamelCamel (for Amazon) to track historical lows.
Make a wishlist in advance so you can add items to cart quickly when sales go live.
Expect stock-outs on best-sellers within 24 to 48 hours of Black Friday going live.
Compare final prices after tax and shipping: a 15 percent discount with free shipping often beats 20 percent with a ~$15 to 25 shipping charge.

sections.tip: Black Friday 2025 and 2026 will fall around Nov. 25 to 29. Cyber Monday follows a few days later. Set a calendar reminder for mid-September to start tracking prices.

sections.h2: Post-Holiday Winter Sales (December to early January)

sections.p: December sees two overlapping sales patterns. First, pre-Christmas promotions run from early December through Dec. 20 or so, as retailers push inventory before year-end. These are often weaker than Black Friday: 10 to 15 percent discounts are typical. Then, after Christmas (Dec. 26 onward), post-holiday clearance kicks in as retailers make room for new stock arriving in January. This second wave often yields deeper discounts than Black Friday, sometimes reaching 25 to 35 percent, but selection narrows because popular items are already gone.

January sales are driven by annual inventory resets. Manufacturers often release new firmware, minor hardware revisions, or updated SKUs early in the year, so older stock needs to clear. If a wheel or pedal set has been out for 18 months or longer, January is when you will see meaningful markdowns. This is also when new-year gym memberships and racing leagues drive casual interest, so retailers stock up and then discount to clear overstocks by February.

list: Watch for Dec. 26 to Jan. 10 for the deepest winter clearance discounts.
Earlier January (Jan. 1 to 10) tends to offer better selection; later January (Jan. 15 to 31) has deeper discounts but fewer SKUs.
Check if manufacturers are releasing new products or firmware updates in January or February, which signals older models will be discounted.
Free shipping offers are common in January because retailers want to close out inventory, so the total price is often lower than the discount percentage suggests.

sections.h2: Spring and Summer Lulls (March to August)

sections.p: March through August is the slowest sales period for sim racing hardware. Retail discounts shrink to 5 to 15 percent, and they are often scattered across random dates rather than coordinated sales events. This is when brand loyalty and patience pay off. Smaller retailers and direct-to-consumer channels (manufacturer websites) occasionally run flash sales or clearance events on overstock, but you have to watch them actively.

The exception is Easter (late March or April), which sometimes triggers a week-long promotional push from major retailers. It is worth checking in mid-March, but discounts rarely exceed those in January. Summer's heat also coincides with lower demand for indoor sim racing, so manufacturers and retailers have less pressure to discount aggressively. If you need new gear in this window, prioritize direct-manufacturer deals and email newsletters that announce private sales to subscribers.

olist: Subscribe to manufacturer email lists (MOZA, Fanatec, Thrustmaster) in January or February so you receive private sale notifications.
Check discount code sites like RetailMeNot and Honey in May and June for subscriber-only or seasonal coupons.
Watch for end-of-quarter sales (June 30, Sept. 30) when retailers discount to hit quarterly targets.
Consider buying used gear in this period: many casual racers sell equipment after winter leagues end, and prices on the secondhand market dip accordingly.

sections.tip: Spring is when new racing seasons begin in many sims. Expect price stability rather than discounts unless overstock is a problem.

sections.h2: Back-to-School and Early Fall (August to September)

sections.p: Late August and September see a minor uptick in sim racing sales tied to back-to-school shopping and the start of new iRacing seasons. Retailers run modest discounts (10 to 20 percent) to capture this wave, but they are not aggressive because the market is smaller than Black Friday or holiday seasons. Amazon Prime Day in mid-July sometimes includes sim racing gear, but discounts are unpredictable and vary by product.

September is a better opportunity than August. By early September, retailers begin stocking inventory for the holiday season, and they often discount older or overstock items to make shelf space. Additionally, any manufacturer releasing new products or firmware updates in September needs to clear 2024 to 2025 models. If you are patient until late September, you can sometimes catch clearance pricing on established gear before Black Friday pricing schemes take over in October.

The strategy depends on when you need or want the gear. If you are upgrading or building a rig for a specific league season or event, work backward from that deadline and anchor your purchase to the nearest major sale window. If you have flexibility, aim for January or late September through early October. These windows offer better discounts than summer and spring, but less marketing hype and stock pressure than Black Friday.

Track your gear wishlist in a spreadsheet with baseline prices, then monitor for sales. Use price-tracking tools to automate alerts so you do not have to check manually every week. Set a threshold: decide in advance what discount percentage (e.g., 20 percent) or dollar amount (e.g., save ~$100 on a wheelbase) would justify a purchase. This removes emotion and helps you avoid impulse buys disguised as deals.

list: Build a wishlist with model numbers, baseline prices, and your target discount percentage.
Use CamelCamelCamel for Amazon, Honey, or Keepa to track historical price lows and set alerts.
Check manufacturer websites directly for seasonal coupon codes or subscriber-only sales.
Factor in shipping costs and import duties if buying from international retailers.
Consider refurbished or open-box gear from authorized retailers for 15 to 30 percent savings year-round, especially for pedals and cockpit frames.

sections.p: Retailers often discount bundles (wheelbase plus wheel plus pedals) more aggressively than individual components. A MOZA R9 might be 15 percent off standalone, but a R9 plus CS V2 wheel bundle could be 20 to 25 percent off. This is because bundles clear more inventory per transaction. If you are building a new rig from scratch, bundled pricing often saves more money than buying the best individual sales across different dates. Compare bundle prices against buying each item separately even if one piece is not on sale.

Similarly, buying within the same brand ecosystem sometimes triggers additional discounts. A MOZA wheelbase paired with MOZA pedals and MOZA wheel may qualify for a bundle discount that a mixed-brand setup (MOZA wheelbase, Fanatec pedals, Thrustmaster wheel) does not. This is not always obvious until you add items to cart, so test it during major sales events.

sections.tip: Bundle pricing is most aggressive during Black Friday, January clearance, and end-of-quarter sales. Check bundles first, then compare against individual prices.

sections.h2: What to Avoid and When to Buy Regardless

sections.p: Some hardware does not follow seasonal discounts reliably. Limited-run items, new product launches, and high-end racing wheels often stay at MSRP or close to it even during major sales. If you want a specific new release, do not wait for a discount: manufacturers and retailers often keep new products at full price for the first 3 to 6 months. Expect discounts only after the initial demand wave settles.

Conversely, do not wait indefinitely for a sale if your current setup is broken or missing a critical component. Downtime costs more in league points and practice time than a ~10 percent premium paid outside of a sale window. A pedal set at full price today beats waiting three months for a sale and missing two racing seasons. The goal is to optimize spending, not to minimize it at the cost of usability.

faqs.q: Is Black Friday the best time to buy sim racing gear?
faqs.a: Black Friday offers the broadest selection of discounts across multiple brands, but the percentages (typically 10 to 20 percent) are modest. January and late September often have deeper discounts (20 to 35 percent) on older stock, though with smaller selection. Black Friday is best if you want to compare multiple brands at once; January is better if you can wait and want the lowest total price.

faqs.q: Should I buy used or wait for a sale on new gear?
faqs.a: New gear on sale is usually the better value because you get a warranty and full condition. Used gear can save 20 to 40 percent but carries risk if it has hidden wear. Buy new on sale if you have flexibility; buy used only if the specific model you want is no longer discounted new and you have checked the secondhand market price.

faqs.q: When do manufacturers release new products or firmware updates?
faqs.a: Most manufacturers release new products or major firmware updates in January, June, or September to align with new racing seasons or major retail events. If a product was released 18+ months ago, expect discounts when new versions launch. Check manufacturer roadmaps in November to anticipate January updates.

faqs.q: Is there a best month to buy if I need gear right now?
faqs.a: If you need gear within 2 to 3 weeks, check current prices at three major retailers and set up Honey or CamelCamelCamel price alerts for 1 to 2 weeks out. Mid-month discounts are rare, but random flash sales happen weekly. If no meaningful discount appears within two weeks, buy at the current lowest price. Do not wait more than 3 weeks because the opportunity cost of missing practice or league races outweighs a small potential discount.
